extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy; readers studying Kant's Critique of Judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Kant's evaluative criteria for aesthetic judgements (taste, beauty, pleasant, good), including disinterestedness, universality, and the free play of cognitive faculties. Useful for analysing or producing philosophical accounts of aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste is aesthetical
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste refers a representation not by the Understanding to the object for cognition but by the Imagination (perhaps with the Understanding) to the subject and its feeling of pleasure or pain; therefore it is not a judgement of cognition (not logical) but aesthetical — its determining ground can be no other than subjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that unlike cognitive judgements (which refer representations objectively to the object), judgements of taste refer representations to the subject’s feeling; they add nothing to cognition and are not based on concepts. Contrast with objective (cognitive) reference; note role of Imagination and possible conjunction with Understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction determining judgement of taste must be disinterested
rubrics_metrics.description: When we judge something as beautiful, the satisfaction involved must be entirely disinterested — i.e. indifferent to the object’s existence or to any personal or practical interest in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant illustrates by examples (a palace admired in Paris, an Iroquois pleased by cook-shops, Rousseau criticizing vanity) and the thought-experiment of being on an uninhabited island; a judgement of beauty that mixes any interest is partial and not a pure judgement of taste. One must exclude both sensory inclinations and practical concerns (use, possession, social status) to form a pure aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasantness is bound up with interest
rubrics_metrics.description: What pleases the senses (the Pleasant) is tied to sensation and thus to inclination and desire; pleasure of this sort excites desire for the object and depends on the object’s relation to the subject’s state (i.e. interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant distinguishes objective sensation (perception of green meadows) from subjective sensation (feeling of pleasantness). Judging something pleasant implies inclination and often no reflective judgement about the object's character; intense gratification may dispense with judgement altogether. This is contrasted with beauty, which does not presuppose such interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good (moral/practical) is bound up with interest via concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: That which pleases through the mere concept (the Good) involves the idea of purpose and the relation of Reason to volition; to find something good one needs a concept of what the object ought to be, hence interest and connection to will are involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes mediate good (useful) and good in itself (moral good). Unlike the beautiful, the Good is concept-dependent: Reason evaluates objects with reference to purposes and volition. Examples: health is immediately pleasant but judged good insofar as Reason sees its purposive value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three distinct relations to pleasure: Pleasant, Beautiful, Good
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasant, Beautiful, and Good designate three different relations of representations to the feeling of pleasure and pain: the Pleasant gratifies (arouses inclination), the Beautiful merely pleases (disinterested satisfaction), and the Good is esteemed or approved (object of Reason and will).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant emphasizes this tripartite distinction to prevent conflation (e.g., equating lasting pleasure with the good). He notes their different domains (pleasant for animals, beauty for humans as animal+rational, good for rational beings) and that only the beautiful presents a free, disinterested satisfaction (favour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste defined as faculty of disinterested judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is the faculty of judging an object or method of representing it by an entirely disinterested satisfaction or dissatisfaction; the object of such satisfaction is called beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Kant’s compact definition: taste is not about desire or concept-based approval but about an impartial, contemplative response. It reiterates the need for indifference to existence and to practical uses when judging beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: The beautiful pleases universally without a concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful is that which, apart from concepts, is represented as the object of a universal satisfaction — i.e. it pleases universally while not resting on concepts of the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From disinterestedness follows the belief that one’s pleasure in the object could be shared by everyone; because the satisfaction does not depend on private inclinations or concepts, the judge imputes a claim of universal validity (a 'universal voice') to aesthetic judgements even though this universality is not concept-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic universality is subjective (not logical/objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality claimed in judgements of taste is subjective: a general validity of the feeling of pleasure (valid for all subjects), not an objective universal validity grounded in concepts about the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant contrasts subjective universal validity (aesthetical) with objective universal validity (logical, concept-grounded). Aesthetic universality imputes a general communicability of one’s state of mind without providing conceptual reasons that would allow others to be compelled by argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgements of taste are singular yet claim universal validity
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste is, in logical quantity, a singular judgement (it refers to a single representation) but carries an aesthetical claim of universality — the judge expects assent from everyone even though no concept-based rule enforces it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: calling a particular rose beautiful is singular, but one can form a derived general judgement ('Roses in general are beautiful') only by conceptualising multiple singular judgements. Kant warns that while the claim to universal agreement is asserted, the judgement itself cannot, by conceptual means, prove that claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste of Sense vs Taste of Reflection (private vs public claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes taste of Sense (private judgements of pleasure dependent on individual sensation) from taste of Reflection (aesthetical judgements that purport to be generally valid and thus public), both being aesthetic but differing in claim to universality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste of Sense allows 'it is pleasant to me' and accepts private variability (e.g., canary wine pleasant to one, not to another). Taste of Reflection claims a 'universal' satisfaction and demands agreement; misuse of 'beautiful' when only private pleasure is present is a category error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal communicability of the mental state as the basis of aesthetic claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjective condition that grounds the judgement of taste is the mental state's universal communicability — specifically the state of free play of the Imagination and the Understanding in relation to cognition in general, which makes the pleasure universally shareable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues that only what can be communicated (cognition/representation) can ground universality; because the free play of Imagination and Understanding is the subjective condition suitable for cognition in general, its felt harmony is taken as communicable and grounds the claim that others should share the pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure follows the aesthetic judgement; free play of faculties precedes pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: In a judgement of taste the subjective representation of the object's capacity for universal communicability (the free play of Imagination and Understanding) is primary, and the pleasure in the object is consequent — i.e., the judgement (awareness of harmonious free play) precedes and grounds the pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant rejects the view that pre-existing pleasure is merely reported as universal; instead the perceived universal communicability of the cognitive state (free play) produces the pleasure. The free play is felt as a lively harmonious activity of Imagination and Understanding, not as a conceptual cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness (formal purposiveness) as a reflective principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Purposiveness is the representation of an object as if its form were directed to a purpose; purposiveness can appear without presupposing an actual purpose (i.e., purposiveness without purpose) when we explain an object's form by conceiving it 'as if' produced by a will or idea of a purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant introduces purposiveness transcendentaly: a purpose is when an object is thought as caused by a concept (forma finalis); yet we can observe purposiveness of form by reflection without assuming an actual end or will. This notion will be used to relate aesthetic judgements to a sense of purposiveness in nature or art.
